newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: ADNOC details Ruwais oil refinery development.
newsitem.headline: ADNOC details Ruwais oil refinery development.

text.p: Two condensate processing trains at Abu Dhabi's Ruwais oil refinery are expected to come onstream six months apart in 1999, a paper prepared by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) said on Monday.

"In the first phase of the Ruwais Expansion and Upgrading Master (EUM) plan, two condensate processing trains, each 140,000 barrels per day (bpd), with attendant kerosene sweetening units and naphtha stabilisers will be implemented," said a conference paper by ADNOC's processing directorate.
Plans to upgrade and expand Ruwais, Abu Dhabi's main refinery, have been revised and the paper was one of the first official confirmations of the nature and scope of plant work.
The condensate trains will be needed to process additional condensate production from local onshore gas field developments.
"The trains are expected to come onstream six months apart during 1999, followed by unleaded gasoline production facilities and a gas oil hydrotreater to reduce sulphur," the paper said.
"Gasoline production units include a naphtha hydrotreater, a 27,500 bpd catalytic reformer with provision for future para-xylene production and a 25,000 bpd isomerisation unit."

A second phase expansion of Ruwais would double the plant's capacity with the installation of a 135,000 bpd crude distillation train, a hydrocracker, gas oil hydrotreaters and residue upgrading and associated downstream units.
The second phase is expected to be completed between 2002-2003, industry analysts said.

"In addition to processing the large volumes (about 280,000 bpd) of condensate available from the onshore gas development projects, it (EUM) includes facilities to double crude oil processing capacity," the ADNOC paper, presented at the fifth annual Middle East Petroleum and Gas Conference said.

Work at Ruwais and the development of new smaller refineries in other emirates of the United Arab Emirates is likely to push the country's crude distillation refining capacity from a current 250,000 bpd to 319,000 bpd by 2000, according to forecasts given at the conference by the Seattle Research and Training Center (SRTC).
